You might think asking an AI chatbot for medical advice is obviously a bad idea, but hundreds of millions of people do so every week.

In a nearly fatal case—now the subject of a lawsuit—ChatGPT advised a priest to ignore the symptoms of a pulmonary embolism, a condition with a 30% mortality rate. The chatbot's advice likely made things worse…

AI chatbots are useful for many things, but replacing a doctor isn't one of them. Given that they tend to hallucinate confidently, they're no good substitute for Google searches either.

And yet, even OpenAI's own figures show hundreds of millions of people ask ChatGPT about health issues every week. Similarly, an analysis of Microsoft Copilot search logs found health questions were among the most popular categories in its mobile app.

If you want any proof of the potential consequences of relying on chatbots for medical advice, a lawsuit filed by a Florida priest provides an instructive case. According to The New York Times, he is suing OpenAI because ChatGPT told him not to worry about symptoms of a pulmonary embolism.

ChatGPT told him to just rest. Not only did it advise him not to seek medical help, but staying still for long periods is exactly the worst thing to do in this situation—I say this because I myself experienced a pulmonary embolism years ago after sitting on a 12-hour flight following a broken bone; researchers were aware of this risk at the time but did not inform passengers.

When Winters was finally admitted to intensive care, doctors said his symptoms were most likely caused by a series of pulmonary embolisms, and that his condition had worsened because he had followed ChatGPT's advice and spent weeks sitting still.

The report noted Winters was using GPT-4o, an older version of ChatGPT known for its sycophantic responses. This may explain why the chatbot mentioned trusting in God; but whatever AI model you use, please don't let it provide your medical advice.
